effective_sic4_count.why: separates office from sic2 and KEEPS separating them at equal member count

log10_ebitda_span.why: fails the size-matched control: inside at least one member-count bucket the office cohorts are NOT worse than the sic2 cohorts, so what looked like coherence was the member count

margin_iqr.why: fails the size-matched control: inside at least one member-count bucket the office cohorts are NOT worse than the sic2 cohorts, so what looked like coherence was the member count

top_sic4_share.why: separates office from sic2 and KEEPS separating them at equal member count

effective_sic4_count.definition: 1 / SUM(share_i^2) over the distinct SIC4 codes inside the cohort -- the inverse Herfindahl of its industry composition, i.e. the effective number of DIFFERENT four-digit industries the cohort is made of.
effective_sic4_count.degenerate_at: sic4, where it is 1.00 by construction -- every member shares the code. That is a definitional value and is reported as such; the informative comparison is sic2 against office, where neither value is fixed.
effective_sic4_count.why: A peer group built of 140 effective industries is not a peer group. This is a COMPOSITION statistic: it is scale-free and does not move with the member count on its own -- doubling a cohort by adding more of the same industry leaves it unchanged.

log10_ebitda_span.definition: p90 - p10 of log10(EBITDA) over cohort members with a positive EBITDA -- the cohort's size spread, in DECADES.
log10_ebitda_span.verdict: REJECTED for the same reason, and by a narrower margin: 2.471 decades at office against 2.672 at sic2 among cohorts of the same size. Size dispersion inside ONE four-digit industry is already two decades, so there is little room left for a wider rung to add.
log10_ebitda_span.why: Dispersion of the quantity actually being benchmarked. `ebitda_benchmark` asks what a RIGHT-SIZED peer earns, and a cohort spanning five decades of EBITDA has no right-sized peer to speak of. Logs because EBITDA is heavy-tailed across four orders of magnitude even inside one industry.

margin_iqr.definition: p75 - p25 of the EBITDA margin (EBITDA / revenue) across cohort members whose EBITDA and revenue both resolve at a MATCHED period.
margin_iqr.degenerate_at: nothing -- it is a sample quantile spread at every rung
margin_iqr.verdict: REJECTED -- it separates the rungs over all peer sets and STOPS separating them at equal member count. At 542+ members the office cohorts' median IQR is 0.342 against sic2's 1.427: the office cohort is TIGHTER, because pooling twenty industries pulls the quartiles toward the aggregate centre. A dispersion statistic measures a population's variance, not whether it is one population.
margin_iqr.why: The owner's own test: 'a cohort whose EBITDA margins span three orders of magnitude is not a peer group'. An interquartile spread is a consistent estimator of the population spread, so unlike a range it does not grow with the member count. Whether it SEPARATES the rungs is an empirical question, and `pit_peer_coherence.py` answers it.

top_sic4_share.definition: the share of the cohort's classified members contributed by its single largest SIC4 subgroup.
top_sic4_share.degenerate_at: sic4, where it is 1.00 by construction
top_sic4_share.why: The same composition fact read the other way round, and the one a person can check by eye: 'the biggest single industry in this 800-member peer group is 4% of it' is an argument nobody needs a statistic to follow.

resources.wal_growth_note: This module holds a mode=ro connection and CANNOT write. A WAL that grows during the run is ANOTHER process writing to the same store -- expected on this machine, and reported rather than attributed to this reader.
